name: Transpiration Rate Calculator
seoDesc: Transpiration is water lost through stomata, driven by the vapour pressure difference between leaf and air. Free transpiration rate calculator: enter your val
summary:
Transpiration is water lost through stomata, driven by the vapour pressure difference between leaf and air. It returns transpiration rate, daily water use per m² of leaf, molar rate and approximate stomatal conductance, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator converts a measured loss into a rate per unit leaf area and a whole-plant water use, and links it to the water the roots must supply. The arithmetic keeps full precision internally and only rounds what it displays, so the number you copy out is the number the formula produced. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the Transpiration Rate
sections.html:
Transpiration rate (g/m²/h) = mass lost ÷ leaf area ÷ time in hours

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
masswater lost by the shootg
arealeaf area of the shootm²
ratetranspiration rateg/m²/h

sections.title: How do I use the Transpiration Rate?
sections.html:
Fill the boxes you have numbers for; the calculator decides what it can derive from them.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: mass lost of 2.4 g, leaf area of 0.015 m², duration of 30 min.

Substituting them into the formula gives transpiration rate of 320 g/m²/h, daily water use per m² of leaf of 3.84 L/m²/day, molar rate of 4.94 mmol/m²/s, approximate stomatal conductance of 0.1122 mol/m²/s.

Because the example uses the defaults, you can reproduce it by loading the page and reading the results panel before touching anything.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
Interpretation is a convention, not part of the arithmetic. The usual bands are:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
below 20 g/m²/hLowshade, high humidity or closed stomata
20 – 100Moderatetypical glasshouse conditions
above 100Highbright, dry, windy conditions

  • Mass loss measured by weighing is total evapotranspiration from the shoot; a gas analyser measures the transpiration flux directly.

  • Water lost is water the roots must replace: at 1 L/m²/day a square metre of leaf needs about a litre a day, which scales quickly to whole-canopy irrigation.

  • Transpiration cools the leaf; a water-stressed leaf runs several degrees warmer, which is the principle behind thermal stress indices.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
Before blaming the formula, check these — they explain nearly every mismatch:

  • Weighing the pot rather than the shoot, so evaporation from the substrate is included.
  • Using leaf area measured on one side of the leaf when both are transpiring.
  • Reporting g/h without normalising to leaf area.

faq.q: How do I convert g/m²/h to mmol/m²/s?
faq.a: Divide by 18 (grams per mole of water) and by 3.6.

faq.q: Why does transpiration matter for nutrient uptake?
faq.a: Because mass flow in the xylem is the main route by which nutrients reach the roots.

faq.q: What does the Transpiration Rate actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns transpiration rate, daily water use per m² of leaf, molar rate and approximate stomatal conductance. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
